name: Low Earth Orbit (LEO · 400 km)
goodAt: Very sharp ground detail (0.2–0.3 km) and inexpensive launches via Small or Rideshare slots; two cheap satellites achieve fast revisit.
badAt: Residual upper-atmosphere drag limits a single satellite's life to ~2 years (especially during solar storms) and ground station passes are brief.
hintText: At 400 km you circle Earth every ~92 minutes—great zoom and cheap rockets, but pair with a second satellite or watch atmospheric drag!
sourceLabel: NASA Orbital Debris / Thermospheric Drag at 400 km

name: Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO · 700 km)
goodAt: Crosses every latitude at the same local solar time with global coverage, 7+ year lifetime, and frequent passes over Svalbard and Alaska polar stations.
badAt: Higher altitude than 400 km LEO reduces rocket mass limit slightly and takes ~11.5 hours between repeat observations for a single satellite.
hintText: Real NASA fire-watching satellites like Suomi NPP and Aqua fly in Sun-Synchronous Orbit to compare wildfires under consistent daily lighting.
sourceLabel: NASA Earth Observatory — Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits (SSO)

name: Geostationary Orbit (GEO · 35,786 km)
goodAt: Matches Earth's rotation to hover continuously over one hemisphere—spot fires within minutes and enjoy 24/7 continuous ground contact.
badAt: 35,786 km altitude demands a Medium rocket ($70M), a large 120 Wh battery for 69-minute equinox eclipses, and a specialized telescope to stay under 1 km resolution.
hintText: GEO requires a Medium (Falcon 9 class) rocket and the Wide-Field GEO Telescope; standard LEO cameras become ~27 km blurry from this high up!
sourceLabel: NASA Earth Observatory — Geostationary Orbit Mechanics
